Marina’s jaw tightened. She checked her watch, the second hand ticking loudly in the quiet space. “I don’t have time for thanks, I have a deadline; do you know the answer or not?”

Elliot nodded slowly, maintaining his serene posture. “I completely understand how important it is to stay on schedule, and I certainly want to ensure that you feel supported in your efforts to meet those timelines.”

She grabbed a standard J-hook from her tool belt, holding it up against the bracket. “Support would be telling me if the standard J-hooks will hold the weight or if I need to fabricate new mounts.”

“It is wonderful to see such dedication to safety and structural integrity, and I believe that exploring established safety protocols could be a very valuable next step for your project,” Elliot replied, his tone light and encouraging.

Marina slammed the hook back into her belt. “I’ve read the protocols, they’re useless for custom retrofits; are you saying you have no idea how to secure these cables?”

Elliot tilted his head, listening intently. “I hear your concern about the limitations of general guidelines, and I want to validate that every installation presents its own unique set of challenges that deserve careful consideration.”

“This is ridiculous, I need a technical answer, not validation; who here actually knows the rigging specs?” Marina snapped, her shoulders rising toward her ears.

“It is always helpful to consult with specialized experts who have deep familiarity with the building’s original documentation, and I am sure that reaching out to the maintenance department would yield some interesting insights,” Elliot suggested, his voice steady.

“I can’t wait for them, they’re booked out for weeks; can you just look at the diagram and suggest a path?” she demanded, shoving a folded schematic toward him.

Elliot did not take the paper. Instead, he looked at it with mild interest. “I truly admire your proactive approach to problem-solving, and I think that reviewing the architectural blueprints in the archives might provide a helpful context for your routing decisions.”

“The blueprints are outdated and don’t show the sub-grids; stop stalling and tell me if I should drill or zip-tie.”

“I appreciate your passion for getting the job done correctly, and I would gently suggest that speaking with a licensed electrician could help ensure that the chosen method aligns with current code requirements,” Elliot said, his demeanor unchanged.

Marina stepped back, crossing her arms. “I don’t need a code check, I need a mechanic’s advice; are you refusing to help because you can’t?”

“I value our conversation and the respect you show for the venue’s history, and I hope that continuing to explore those official resources will bring you the clarity you are seeking,” Elliot replied, offering a small, polite bow of his head.

Marina let out a short, bitter laugh. “Fine, keep your secrets; I’ll figure it out myself and hope nothing falls on the set designer.”

Elliot’s smile widened slightly. “Thank you for your understanding and for prioritizing the safety of your team, and I wish you the very best in finding a solution that works for everyone involved.”

Clem gestured to the mixing buckets on the workbench. "It’s the standard two-part clear epoxy, five-to-one ratio. I followed the datasheet exactly. I mixed it for three minutes, scraped the sides, and let it rest for ten to degas. It looked perfect when I poured."

Dalia nodded, absorbing the details. "Sounds like you did the heavy lifting right. I was doing a similar pour last week for a countertop and had to fight the weather. Was it chilly in here last night? That bay door was left ajar for a bit."

"Yeah, you can usually sand that out once it’s fully cured. But you gotta wait for it to harden completely first. Rushing it while it’s still tacky will just smear the chemicals around. I learned that the hard way on a coffee table," she warned.

"It should help buffer the draft. Bees are amazing, really. A honeybee colony can keep the brood nest warm even when it’s freezing outside by huddling together and vibrating. It’s like a biological thermostat," she continued, eyes distant.
